extracted.intended_audience: reporters covering criminal and civil court beats; journalism students learning courtroom reporting
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for reporters on what to include and how to write news stories about criminal and civil court proceedings, with examples showing leads, scene-setting, testimony reporting, and necessary legal/ procedural details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead — beginning of summarized testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: beginning of the first sentence of the summarized testimony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the opening (the beginning of the first sentence) of the summarized testimony as the lead or an anchoring element for the story; start with the most immediate, quotable element of testimony to draw readers into the report.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verdict and conditions under which it was rendered
rubrics_metrics.description: (1) the verdict and the conditions under which it was rendered
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report the jury or judge's verdict and any circumstances affecting it (e.g., unanimity, hung jury, special conditions, procedural context). Example contexts in the text: verdicts read in court, jury deliberation times.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentence imposed
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give the punishment or sentence handed down (length of imprisonment, fines, probation) and note any immediate consequences (e.g., remitted fines, adjournments). The examples show reporting of sentences, fines, and possible ranges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision rendered and its significance
rubrics_metrics.description: (3) the decision rendered and its significance
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State the court's decision or ruling and explain its legal or public importance — why the decision matters beyond the immediate parties (precedent, community impact, policy implications).

rubrics_metrics.name: Important testimony
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summarize or quote the key testimony that influenced the case (direct and cross-examination highlights). The text demonstrates detailed paraphrase and selective Q&A reporting (e.g., long witness examinations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Net results of the day's proceedings in a trial
rubrics_metrics.description: (5) net results of the day’s proceedings in a trial
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consolidate what was accomplished that day (who testified, what rulings were made, what witnesses remain) so readers can follow progress of a multi-day trial; e.g., which witnesses were called and whether intended testimony was reached or postponed.

rubrics_metrics.name: History of the case or action
rubrics_metrics.description: (6) the history of the case or action
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide background and chronology (prior arrests, related suits, previous judgments) that contextualize the current proceedings. Examples in the text include prior convictions, extradition history, earlier suits and appeals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisions of a will
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reporting probate or will disputes, enumerate the will's provisions that are at issue (beneficiaries, bequests, conditions). Include relevant quotes or clauses when necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liabilities, assets, and cause in bankruptcy
rubrics_metrics.description: (8) liabilities, assets, and cause in bankruptcy
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In bankruptcy or insolvency reporting, list the debtor's assets and liabilities and the stated cause of bankruptcy; explain the financial implications for creditors and stakeholders.

rubrics_metrics.name: The award or finding
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record the court or jury's award (damages, compensation) or factual finding; include amounts and any conditions attached to the award.

rubrics_metrics.name: The grounds on which a suit is based
rubrics_metrics.description: (10) the grounds on which a suit is based
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain the legal basis or claims underlying the suit (cause of action, statutory or common-law grounds) so readers understand why the case was brought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use human-interest detail and motive to explain actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Include human motives, family circumstances, and emotive detail to explain why defendants or parties acted as they did.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The examples (e.g., man who forged a check to bury his baby; the newsboy turned counterfeiter) show that reporting personal background, poverty, family reactions, and motives gives readers context and sympathy or understanding. Include quotes from relatives and visible reactions in court.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ scene-setting, description, and characterization
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe the courtroom scene, characters, and sensory details to bring the story to life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use vivid detail (e.g., 'soft patter on the floor', 'tall policeman', 'alley scenes', clothing and gestures) to situate readers and convey atmosphere. The Children's Court and murder-trial narration are models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use direct quotations and reported Q&A selectively
rubrics_metrics.description: Report key direct quotations and selective question-and-answer exchanges from testimony and counsel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quote short, revealing exchanges or summarize longer testimony. The Schepps Q&A and Wilson's transcript-style account show how to isolate and present crucial turns in testimony without reproducing entire examinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report procedural facts: pleas, bail, adjournments, 'bound over' status
rubrics_metrics.description: Include procedural actions such as pleas entered, bail set, adjournments, commitments, and whether a defendant was bound over for trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers need to know the immediate procedural posture (e.g., 'fined $10 or thirty days', 'bail set at $9,000', 'case adjourned one week', 'bound over to Municipal court'). These details frequently appear in the examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include names, ages, addresses and occupations when relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: Record identifying details — full names, ages, addresses, occupations or business locations of parties and witnesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The samples routinely provide street addresses, ages, and occupations (e.g., 'Carl Wilson, 1228 Jenifer Street', 'Moy You Toy, 14, address 34 Mott street'); include such specifics to ground the report and enable public identification where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain potential penalties and legal classification of the charge
rubrics_metrics.description: State the formal charge(s) and the statutory or degree classification and the potential penalty range.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible, note the legal label (e.g., 'grand larceny in the second degree') and the statutory punishment (e.g., 'punishable by imprisonment from one to ten years'), as done in the Grand Larceny and sentencing examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summarize admissions, confessions, and criminal records
rubrics_metrics.description: Highlight defendant admissions, confessions, and relevant criminal records revealed during proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a defendant pleads guilty or admits facts (or a witness confesses), report those admissions and any prior record disclosed on cross-examination, as they materially affect the story and reader understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Note involvement of social agencies and nonlegal remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: Report referrals or commitments to social agencies, guardianship decisions, and noncriminal remedies ordered by the court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Children's Court example shows commitment to the Gerry Society and investigation of guardianship; include such social-service outcomes and follow-up plans when relevant.
